The Story of Parashar the Ascetic

I bow to Lord Jinendra and write the story of an ascetic named Parashar, drawn from the scriptures of other traditions, so that the noble may understand the false conceptions found in those teachings.

In Hastinagpur there lived a fisherman named Gangbhat. One day this sinful man caught a large fish from the river. When he cut it open at home, a beautiful girl emerged. Her body emitted a terrible stench. The fisherman named her Satyvati and raised her. But truly, can a girl be born from a fish? It is regrettable that people blindly believe such things without question.

When Satyvati had grown, one day Gangbhat left her sitting in a boat by the riverbank while he went home on some errand. At that time a weary ascetic named Parashar, travelling along the road, came to where Satyvati sat with her boat. He said, "Girl, I need to cross the river. If you would take me across in your boat, it would be very kind." Innocent Satyvati agreed, seated him in the boat, and began to row. Satyvati was beautiful, and now thirteen or fourteen years old, her youth freshly blossoming. Her loveliness shook the ascetic's austerity. He became a slave to desire and revealed his sinful intentions to Satyvati.

Satyvati was ashamed and frightened. She said, "Maharaj, you are a holy man, one who bathes in the Ganga daily, capable of blessing and cursing — and I am a girl of low birth, my body foul-smelling. How can I be worthy of one such as you?" But Parashar felt no shame at the innocent girl's guileless words — for where do the lustful know shame? He said, "Do not worry about that. I shall make your body fragrant at once." With the power of his learning, he transformed her body so that it became sweetly perfumed. Seeing his power, Satyvati had to agree.

The lustful Parashar wished to satisfy his desire right there in the boat. Satyvati said, "Do you not think of what people will say if they see?" Then Parashar created a fog in the sky so that no one could see them. In this way he fulfilled his desire and departed. From this union, a son was eventually born — who in later tradition became known as the sage Ved Vyas.

This story is told to reveal the moral failings hidden in the legends of other traditions. An ascetic who has practised penance for years abandons everything for a moment of desire — and the tradition that celebrates him calls this holy. The Jain perspective asks: can one who is enslaved to lust be called a true sage? Can one who exploits an innocent girl be worthy of worship? The noble should reflect on such matters with discernment.
